intro.why: Linear regression is the simplest neural network: one neuron, identity activation, squared error and gradient descent. Every later network (logistic and softmax regression in Module 4, deep networks in Module 5) reuses exactly this data–model–loss–optimiser loop.
prereq: Vectors, matrices and the dot product
The four components of a DL problem (Module 1)

symbols: design matrix, one row per example

sections.title: What is regression?
sections.plain: Predict a continuous number from features.
sections.body: Definition (p.4): regression is a supervised learning task that predicts a continuous-valued output based on input features. Key characteristics: input a feature vector $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^d$; output a real-valued target $y\in\mathbb R$; goal: learn a function $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ such that $y\approx f(\mathbf x)$.

sections.title: Examples of regression problems
sections.plain: House prices, temperature, stock prices.
sections.body:
• House price prediction: input size, location, number of rooms; output price in dollars.
  • Temperature forecasting: input historical weather data, season, humidity; output temperature in degrees.
  • Stock price prediction: input historical prices, trading volume, market indicators; output future stock price (p.5).

sections.title: What is linear regression?
sections.plain: Output = weighted sum of inputs + bias.
sections.body:
Definition: linear regression assumes the output is a linear combination of the input features (p.7):

$$y=w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2+\cdots+w_dx_d\qquad(1)$$

where $\mathbf x=[x_1,\dots,x_d]^T$ are the input features, $\mathbf w=[w_1,\dots,w_d]^T$ the weights and $w_0$ the bias term. "Linear" means linear in the parameters: features can be non-linear transformations of raw inputs (basis functions) and the model stays linear regression.

sections.title: Examples of linear regression
sections.plain: Salary, crop yield, energy as weighted sums.
sections.body:
• Salary $=w_0+w_1\times$ years of experience.
  • Crop yield $=w_0+w_1\times$ rainfall $+w_2\times$ fertilizer.
  • Energy $=w_0+w_1\times$ temperature $+w_2\times$ hour $+w_3\times$ day.

The relationship between inputs and output is assumed to be linear (p.8). Each weight reads as "change in output per unit change of that feature, others fixed".

sections.title: The four components
sections.plain: Data, model (one neuron), objective (error), algorithm (GD).
sections.body:
1. Data: $d$-dimensional input vectors and target outputs.
  2. Model: a single neuron implementing a linear function.
  3. Objective function: measures prediction error.
  4. Learning algorithm: gradient descent to optimise the weights (p.10).

sections.title: Matrix form of data
sections.plain: Stack examples as rows of X with a leading 1.
sections.body:
For efficient computation we organise data into matrices (p.11). Augment each input with a bias term $\tilde{\mathbf x}^{(i)}=[1,x_1^{(i)},\dots,x_d^{(i)}]^T$; each row is one training example:

$$X=\begin{bmatrix}1&x_1^{(1)}&\cdots&x_d^{(1)}\\1&x_1^{(2)}&\cdots&x_d^{(2)}\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\1&x_1^{(N)}&\cdots&x_d^{(N)}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{N\times(d+1)},\quad \mathbf y=[y^{(1)},\dots,y^{(N)}]^T\in\mathbb R^N,\quad \mathbf w=[w_0,w_1,\dots,w_d]^T\in\mathbb R^{d+1}.$$

sections.title: Linear model as a single neuron; prediction
sections.plain: ŷ = f(wᵀx) with f(z) = z; vectorised ŷ = Xw.
sections.body:
Model linear regression as a single artificial neuron (p.12): inputs $1,x_1,\dots,x_d$ with weights $w_0,\dots,w_d$ feed a summation $\Sigma$, then activation $f$, giving $\hat y\in\mathbb R$.

$$\hat y=f(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x)=f(w_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2+\cdots+w_dx_d)\quad(2),\qquad \hat{\mathbf y}=X\mathbf w\quad(3)$$

with $\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ the parameters, $\mathbf x=[1,x_1,\dots,x_d]^T$ and $f$ the identity (p.13). Cost of a forward pass over the dataset: $O(Nd)$.

sections.title: Identity activation function
sections.body:
$$f(z)=z\qquad(4)$$

Properties (p.14): output continuous on $(-\infty,\infty)$; differentiable everywhere with $f'(z)=1$; allows any real output; gradient flows unchanged through the neuron; suited to continuous targets. Why identity for regression: targets are continuous (prices, temperatures); we must predict any real number, not just {0, 1}; differentiability enables gradient-based optimisation; no information loss from input to output.

sections.title: Objective: squared-error loss
sections.plain: Half the squared error, averaged over examples.
sections.body:
$$\ell(\mathbf w;\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})=\tfrac12(\hat y^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2=\tfrac12(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2\quad(5)$$$$J(\mathbf w)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac12(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2\quad(6),\qquad \mathbf w^*=\arg\min_{\mathbf w}J(\mathbf w)\quad(7)$$

The ½ cancels the 2 from differentiation; it doesn't change the minimiser (p.15).

sections.title: Why squared error?
sections.plain: Smooth, convex, punishes big errors, Gaussian MLE.
sections.body:
Advantages (p.16): differentiable (smooth everywhere); convex (single global minimum for linear models); penalises large errors (quadratic growth); statistical interpretation (maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise). Vector form:

$$J(\mathbf w)=\frac1{2N}\|X\mathbf w-\mathbf y\|^2=\frac1{2N}(X\mathbf w-\mathbf y)^T(X\mathbf w-\mathbf y)\qquad(8)$$

MLE derivation. If $y=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+\varepsilon$, $\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)$ i.i.d., then $-\log p(\mathbf y\mid X,\mathbf w)=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|X\mathbf w-\mathbf y\|^2+\frac N2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)$; the second term doesn't depend on $\mathbf w$, so maximising likelihood = minimising (8). Convexity: the Hessian $\nabla^2J=\frac1NX^TX$ is positive semi-definite (strictly convex when $X$ has full column rank). Limitation: squared error is sensitive to outliers (MAE or Huber are robust alternatives).

sections.title: Batch gradient descent algorithm
sections.plain: Repeat: gradient on all data, step against it, stop when small.
sections.body:
Algorithm 1: Gradient descent for linear regression (p.17)
Input:  dataset D = {(x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾)}ᵢ₌₁..N, learning rate η, tolerance ε
Output: learned weights w
1  initialise w⁽⁰⁾ = 0 (or random)
2  t ← 0
3  while not converged do
4      ∇J(w⁽ᵗ⁾) = (1/N) Xᵀ(Xw⁽ᵗ⁾ − y)        # O(Nd)
5      w⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾ = w⁽ᵗ⁾ − η ∇J(w⁽ᵗ⁾)
6      if ‖∇J(w⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾)‖ < ε then break      # converged
7      t ← t + 1
8  return w⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾

Complexity: $O(Nd)$ time per iteration, $O(Nd)$ memory for $X$ (plus $O(d)$ for $\mathbf w$). "Batch" means every iteration uses all $N$ examples; mini-batch and stochastic variants appear in Module 4.

sections.title: Computing the gradient
sections.plain: ∇J = (1/N) Xᵀ(Xw − y).
sections.body:
$$ abla J(\mathbf w)= rac{\partial J}{\partial\mathbf w}= rac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x^{(i)}-y^{(i)})\,\mathbf x^{(i)}\quad(9),\qquad abla J(\mathbf w)= rac1NX^T(X\mathbf w-\mathbf y)\quad(10)$$

with $X^T\in\mathbb R^{(d+1) imes N}$ and $X\mathbf w-\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^N$, so $ abla J\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$ (p.18).

Derivation. For one example, by the chain rule $ rac{\partial\ell}{\partial w_j}=(\hat y-y)\cdot rac{\partial\hat y}{\partial w_j}=(\hat y-y)\,f'(z)\,x_j=(\hat y-y)x_j$ since $f'(z)=1$. Averaging over examples gives (9); stacking the $N$ error terms into $\mathbf e=X\mathbf w-\mathbf y$ gives (10). Equivalently, expand (8): $J= rac1{2N}(\mathbf w^TX^TX\mathbf w-2\mathbf y^TX\mathbf w+\mathbf y^T\mathbf y)$ and differentiate. Setting (10) to zero gives the normal equations $X^TX\mathbf w=X^T\mathbf y$.

sections.title: Gradient-descent update rule
sections.plain: w ← w − (η/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y); η too big overshoots, too small is slow.
sections.body:
$$\mathbf w^{(t+1)}=\mathbf w^{(t)}-\frac{\eta}{N}X^T(X\mathbf w^{(t)}-\mathbf y)\qquad(11)$$

Key parameters (p.19): learning rate $\eta$ controls the step size (too large may overshoot the minimum; too small converges slowly); stopping criterion $\|\nabla J(\mathbf w)\|<\epsilon$ or a maximum number of iterations.

Stability. Since $J$ is quadratic with Hessian $H=\frac1NX^TX$, the error $\mathbf w^{(t)}-\mathbf w^*$ evolves as $(I-\eta H)^t$. GD converges iff $0<\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}(H)$; the rate is governed by the condition number $\kappa=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$, roughly $O(\kappa\log(1/\epsilon))$ iterations.

sections.plain: Sizes 1, 2, 3 → prices 2, 4, 5.
sections.body:

$$X=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{3\times2},\quad \mathbf y=\begin{bmatrix}2\\4\\5\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^3,\quad \mathbf w=\begin{bmatrix}w_0\\w_1\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^2\quad(\text{p.21})$$

sections.title: Numerical example: initialisation
sections.plain: w = 0, predictions 0, J = 7.5.
sections.body:
Hyperparameters $\eta=0.1$, $N=3$; $\mathbf w^{(0)}=[0,0]^T$; $\hat{\mathbf y}^{(0)}=X\mathbf w^{(0)}=[0,0,0]^T$ (p.22):

$$J(\mathbf w^{(0)})=\frac16\left\|\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2\\4\\5\end{bmatrix}\right\|^2=\frac16(4+16+25)=7.5.$$

(The slide writes the prediction as $[0\ 0]\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&3\end{bmatrix}$, i.e. $\mathbf w^TX^T$, the same numbers transposed.)

sections.title: Numerical example: gradient
sections.body: $$\mathbf e^{(0)}=\hat{\mathbf y}^{(0)}-\mathbf y=\begin{bmatrix}-2\\-4\\-5\end{bmatrix},\qquad \nabla J(\mathbf w^{(0)})=\frac1NX^T\mathbf e^{(0)}=\frac13\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2\\-4\\-5\end{bmatrix}=\frac13\begin{bmatrix}-2-4-5\\-2-8-15\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3.67\\-8.33\end{bmatrix}\ (\text{p.23})$$

sections.title: Numerical example: weight update
sections.body: $$\mathbf w^{(1)}=\mathbf w^{(0)}-\eta\nabla J(\mathbf w^{(0)})=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}-0.1\begin{bmatrix}-3.67\\-8.33\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0.367\\0.833\end{bmatrix},\qquad \hat{\mathbf y}^{(1)}=X\mathbf w^{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}1.20\\2.03\\2.87\end{bmatrix}\ (\text{p.24})$$

sections.title: Numerical example: new loss
sections.plain: J drops 7.5 → 1.51 (80% lower) after one step.
sections.body:
$$\mathbf e^{(1)}=\hat{\mathbf y}^{(1)}-\mathbf y=\begin{bmatrix}-0.80\\-1.97\\-2.13\end{bmatrix},\qquad J(\mathbf w^{(1)})=\frac16\|\mathbf e^{(1)}\|^2=\frac16(0.64+3.88+4.54)\approx1.51$$

Progress (p.25): initial loss 7.5, after one iteration 1.51: an 80% reduction. Continue until $\|\nabla J\|<\epsilon$ or the maximum iterations. Continuing (code ex1): $J=0.322$ after 2 steps, $0.086$ after 3, and convergence to the least-squares solution $\mathbf w^*=(0.667,1.5)$ with $J^*=0.0278$. For this $X$, $\lambda_{\max}(X^TX/N)=5.55$, so any $\eta>0.36$ diverges.

sections.title: Computational graph for one GD step
sections.plain: w, X → ŷ → e → J; backward e → ∇J → w⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾.
sections.body: Forward (p.26): parameters $\mathbf w^{(t)}$ and input data $X$ meet at a multiply node giving $\hat{\mathbf y}$; subtracting targets $\mathbf y$ gives $\mathbf e$; $\|\cdot\|^2$ gives the loss $J(\mathbf w)$. Backward (dashed): $\frac1N\mathbf e$ is multiplied by $X^T$ to give $\nabla J$, which, scaled by $-\eta$, produces the updated $\mathbf w^{(t+1)}$. This is backpropagation through a one-neuron graph; Module 5 generalises it to many layers.

sections.title: Model evaluation: training vs test error
sections.plain: Learn on train, judge on unseen test data.
sections.body:
Key principle: evaluate on unseen data (p.28). Data split: training set used to learn $\mathbf w$ (typically 90–99%); test set used to evaluate generalisation (typically 1–10%). (Those percentages suit very large datasets; with small data 70–80/20–30 splits or cross-validation are common.)

$$J_{train}=\frac1{N_{train}}\sum_{i\in train}(\hat y^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2,\qquad J_{test}=\frac1{N_{test}}\sum_{i\in test}(\hat y^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2$$

Goal: minimise test error (generalisation performance). A validation split is used for choosing $\eta$, features and stopping time, so the test set stays untouched.

sections.title: Evaluation metrics: MSE, RMSE, MAE
sections.plain: Squared, root-squared and absolute average errors.
sections.body:
$$\text{MSE}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(\hat y^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2\ (12),\qquad \text{RMSE}=\sqrt{\text{MSE}}=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N(\hat y^{(i)}-y^{(i)})^2}\ (13),\qquad \text{MAE}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N|y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)}|\ (14)$$

MAE is less sensitive to outliers than MSE (p.29). RMSE is in the target's units. Note that the training objective $J$ is MSE/2.

sections.title: R² score (coefficient of determination)
sections.plain: Fraction of variance explained, relative to predicting the mean.
sections.body:
$$R^2=1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^N(y^{(i)}-\hat y^{(i)})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^N(y^{(i)}-\bar y)^2}=1-\frac{SS_{residual}}{SS_{total}},\qquad \bar y=\frac1N\sum_iy^{(i)}\qquad(15)$$

Interpretation (p.30): $R^2=1$ perfect fit; $R^2=0$ no better than predicting the mean; $R^2<0$ worse than that baseline (possible on a test set); typically $0.7

sections.title: Tips: learning rate and stopping
sections.plain: Try η on a log grid; stop on small gradient, small change, max iterations or rising validation loss.
sections.body:
1. Choosing η (p.32): start with $\eta\in\{0.001,0.01,0.1,1.0\}$; plot loss vs iterations for each; if loss increases or becomes NaN, decrease $\eta$; if convergence is too slow, increase it; use learning-rate schedules for fine-tuning.

2. When to stop: gradient magnitude $\|\nabla J\|<\epsilon$ (e.g. $10^{-4}$); loss change $|J^{(t)}-J^{(t-1)}|<\epsilon$; maximum iterations (e.g. $T=1000$ or $10{,}000$); validation loss starts increasing (early stopping against overfitting).

sections.title: Tips: initialisation, feature engineering, scaling
sections.plain: Zero init is fine; build meaningful features; standardise.
sections.body:
3. Weight initialisation (p.33): zero initialisation $\mathbf w^{(0)}=\mathbf 0$ works well for linear regression (convex problem, no symmetry issue with one neuron); avoid large initial values (divergence or overflow). 4. Feature engineering: domain knowledge for meaningful derived features (e.g. price per sq ft); feature selection to remove irrelevant/redundant features. 5. Feature scaling and normalisation: features on different scales slow convergence.

$$\text{Min–max: } x'_j=\frac{x_j-\min(x_j)}{\max(x_j)-\min(x_j)}\in[0,1],\qquad \text{Standardisation: } x'_j=\frac{x_j-\mu_j}{\sigma_j}$$

Why it works: scaling reduces the condition number of $X^TX$ (code ex2: $4.6\times10^7$ raw vs 12.6 standardised), so one learning rate suits all directions. Compute $\mu_j,\sigma_j$ on the training set only and reuse them for test data.

sections.title: Debugging checklist
sections.plain: NaN → η too big or unscaled; oscillating → lower η; flat → raise η or fix gradient; test ≫ train → overfitting.
sections.body:
SymptomLikely causesFix
Loss is NaN/InfLearning rate too large; numerical overflow (feature scales)Decrease η, scale features
Loss oscillatingLearning rate too largeDecrease η or use learning-rate decay
Loss not decreasingLearning rate too small; bug in gradient (check signs); wrong sign in update (should be minus)Increase η, verify code (gradient check)
Training works but test error highOverfitting (too many features relative to data)Regularisation, more data, simpler model

(p.34) A numerical gradient check compares (10) with $\frac{J(\mathbf w+h\mathbf e_j)-J(\mathbf w-h\mathbf e_j)}{2h}$.

sections.title: Summary and key takeaways
sections.plain: Data → model → MSE → GD loop; scale features; test on unseen data.
sections.body:
Putting it together (p.36): (1) data and initialisation $\mathcal D=\{(\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}$, $\mathbf w^{(0)}=\mathbf 0$ → forward → (2) model: inputs, Σ, linear activation, $\hat y$ → compute → (3) objective: MSE loss $J(\mathbf w)$ → gradient → (4) learning: $\mathbf w^{(t)}\xrightarrow{-\eta\nabla J}\mathbf w^{(t+1)}$ → iterate. This framework extends to neural networks and deep learning.

Key takeaways (p.37): regression predicts continuous outputs; linear regression assumes $y=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+w_0$; a single neuron with identity activation implements it; squared-error loss is convex; gradient descent iterates $\mathbf w\leftarrow\mathbf w-\eta\nabla J$; feature scaling is critical for fast convergence; evaluation on a test set ensures generalisation. Recap (p.38): problem $y\in\mathbb R$; model a single neuron with identity activation; output $\hat y=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x\in(-\infty,\infty)$; loss MSE; training batch GD.

sections.title: Closed form vs gradient descent
sections.plain: The normal equation solves it in one shot; GD scales better.
sections.body:
Setting $\nabla J=0$ gives $\mathbf w^*=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y$ (covered in ML Module 3). For the worked example: $X^TX=\begin{bmatrix}3&6\\6&14\end{bmatrix}$, $X^T\mathbf y=\begin{bmatrix}11\\25\end{bmatrix}$, $\mathbf w^*=(0.667,1.5)$.

Normal equationGradient descent
Cost$O(Nd^2+d^3)$ once$O(Nd)$ per iteration
HyperparametersNoneη, iterations
Large $d$ (≥10⁴)Slow / memory-heavyFine
Streaming / huge $N$Needs all dataMini-batch/SGD works
Extends to non-linear netsNoYes

Misconceptions. "Linear regression can't model curves": it can, with non-linear features. "R² = 0.95 means the model is right": it can still be biased or extrapolate badly; check residual plots. "Zero init fails": only for hidden layers of multi-layer nets (symmetry), not for a single neuron.

code.title: The slides' gradient-descent example, to convergence
code.explain: Reproduces p.21–25 exactly (∇J = (−3.67, −8.33), w⁽¹⁾ = (0.367, 0.833), J 7.5 → 1.51), runs to convergence, compares with least squares and shows the stability limit η < 2/λ_max.
mistakes: Forgetting the column of ones (no bias).
Dividing by N twice, or not at all, when comparing with the slides.
code.notes: In PyTorch the same model is nn.Linear(d, 1) with nn.MSELoss() and torch.optim.SGD(lr=0.1).
code.code:
# The session's worked example: batch gradient descent for a single linear neuron (NumPy)
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=4, suppress=True)
X = np.array([[1, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3]], float)    # design matrix with the bias column (p.21)
y = np.array([2, 4, 5], float)
N = len(y); eta = 0.1
J = lambda w: ((X @ w - y) ** 2).sum() / (2 * N)  # eq. (8)
w = np.zeros(2)
print(f"t=0: w = {w}  J = {J(w):.4f}")
for t in range(1, 1001):
    e = X @ w - y                                 # error vector
    g = X.T @ e / N                               # eq. (10)
    w = w - eta * g                               # eq. (11)
    if t <= 3 or t in (10, 100, 1000):
        print(f"t={t}: grad = {g}  w = {w}  y_hat = {X @ w}  J = {J(w):.4f}")
    if np.linalg.norm(g) < 1e-6: print(f"converged at t={t}"); break
w_ls = np.linalg.solve(X.T @ X, X.T @ y)          # closed form, for comparison
print("least-squares solution:", w_ls, " J* =", round(J(w_ls), 4))
lam = np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X / N); print("eigenvalues of X^T X / N:", lam, " largest stable eta = 2/lambda_max =", round(2 / lam.max(), 3))
for eta in (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 0.35, 0.4, 1.0):
    w = np.zeros(2)
    for _ in range(100): w -= eta * X.T @ (X @ w - y) / N
    print(f"eta={eta:<5}: J after 100 iterations = {J(w):.4g}")

code.title: Train/test metrics and feature scaling
code.explain: Synthetic house data: LinearRegression with MSE/RMSE/MAE/R² on train and test, then gradient descent on raw vs standardised features.
mistakes: Fitting the scaler on the full dataset (leaks test statistics).
code.notes: Wrap scaler + model in a sklearn Pipeline so the same transform is applied at prediction time.
code.code:
# Train/test evaluation, metrics and feature scaling for linear regression (scikit-learn + NumPy GD)
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, SGDRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_error, r2_score
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 500
size = rng.uniform(600, 3000, n); rooms = np.clip(np.round(size / 600 + rng.normal(0, 0.7, n)), 1, 6)
age = rng.uniform(0, 50, n)
price = 0.12 * size + 15 * rooms - 0.8 * age + 50 + rng.normal(0, 25, n)        # $K, synthetic
X = np.c_[size, rooms, age]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, price, test_size=0.2, random_state=0)
lr = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr)
for name, Xs, ys in (("train", Xtr, ytr), ("test", Xte, yte)):
    p = lr.predict(Xs)
    print(f"{name}: MSE {mean_squared_error(ys, p):8.2f}  RMSE {np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(ys, p)):6.2f}  MAE {mean_absolute_error(ys, p):6.2f}  R2 {r2_score(ys, p):.3f}")
print("weights:", np.round(lr.coef_, 3), "bias:", round(lr.intercept_, 2))
# Gradient descent with and without scaling
def gd(Xm, y, eta, iters=2000):
    A = np.c_[np.ones(len(Xm)), Xm]; w = np.zeros(A.shape[1])
    for t in range(iters):
        g = A.T @ (A @ w - y) / len(y)
        if not np.all(np.isfinite(g)): return t, np.inf
        w -= eta * g
    return iters, ((A @ w - y) ** 2).mean() / 2
sc = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr)
for name, Xm, eta in (("raw features", Xtr, 1e-7), ("raw features", Xtr, 1e-6), ("standardised", sc.transform(Xtr), 0.1)):
    t, J = gd(Xm, ytr, eta)
    print(f"GD {name:13s} eta={eta:<6g}: " + (f"diverged after {t} iterations" if not np.isfinite(J) else f"J = {J:.2f} after {t} iterations"))
print(f"optimum J = {((lr.predict(Xtr) - ytr) ** 2).mean() / 2:.2f}")
A = np.c_[np.ones(len(Xtr)), Xtr]; print("condition number raw: %.2e" % np.linalg.cond(A.T @ A), " standardised: %.1f" % np.linalg.cond(np.c_[np.ones(len(Xtr)), sc.transform(Xtr)].T @ np.c_[np.ones(len(Xtr)), sc.transform(Xtr)]))
sgd = SGDRegressor(max_iter=1000, tol=1e-4, random_state=0).fit(sc.transform(Xtr), ytr)
print("SGDRegressor test R2 (standardised):", round(r2_score(yte, sgd.predict(sc.transform(Xte))), 3))
